doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

title: Arranging as an inventive process and learning music like a language
summary: The joy of a blank page and how a lifetime of listening becomes musical vocabulary.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well I have just enjoyed this conversation so much.
You’re a wealth of — I mean I’m like — arranging to me is, I don’t have the adjective for it but it’s a wonderful occupation and it’s something that I think keeps your brain cells moving.

Yes. You’re right. I mean you know the way I look at it is you’re faced with a blank piece of paper and now you’ve got to put notes, you’ve got to put things on there that are going to sound nice. So it’s a very inventive process. So I still, I’m still just as enthused whenever there’s another arrangement that comes about, figuring how I’m going to go about it. You know it’s a joy, it really is a joy.

I think it’s a craft that all the music you’ve heard in your life can come out in your arrangements. And that, there’s something about that that makes it worthwhile, even the bad gigs you’ve played or the Catskills gigs, it’s still in there and becomes useful.

Yeah. Well the way I explain it to someone who asks about how do you do that, what I tell them is that in the course of your life you’re listening all the time and think of it as learning a language. When you’re a kid and you’re learning a language first you’ve got to learn what the letters stand for, and as you develop, as your vocabulary develops you can speak more clearly and be understood more. Well it’s the same with music. As you learn the sounds that you have, that you hear throughout your life, not only just listening to records and music, but just sounds in general, it all becomes part of your musical vocabulary so that after a while you can speak more clearly and it’s easier to understand what you’re saying.
